note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Prepare and install cable trays - basic

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The specification for a factory job in Spanish Town says 'ladder tray, 300 mm wide, with 25% spare capacity'. What does the spare capacity mean for your planning?
options: The tray may be loaded up to 125% of the maker's stated rating
About a quarter of the space is left free for future cables
A quarter of the supports can be left out on short runs
The tray may be 25% narrower than the drawing shows

questions.stem: The layout drawing shows the tray at 3.0 m above the floor, but the section drawing shows it at 3.4 m. As team leader, what should you do?
options: Fix it at 3.2 m so both drawings are nearly right
Use whichever height is easier to reach from the tower
Fix it at 3.0 m, because the layout drawing comes first
Raise a query and get the height confirmed in writing

questions.stem: Why do you take the other trades' drawings (plumbing, ducts, sprinklers) with you on the site survey for a tray route?
options: To find clashes before any tray is ordered or fixed
To find out which trade will pay for the tray
So the other trades can hang their work on the tray
So the tray can be painted to match the pipes

questions.stem: Which list should you prepare from the drawings before you order tray materials?
options: A cable schedule showing only the cable sizes
A list of the tray maker's other products
A take-off of lengths, fittings, supports and fixings
A list of the tools and ladders held in the Centre's store

questions.stem: A factory wants its tray installed while the staff keep working on the floor below. What is the best plan?
options: Ask the machine operators to watch out for falling tools
Work overhead while staff move around under the tray
Agree work times and set up exclusion zones below the work
Fit the tray as fast as possible so the risk lasts less time

questions.stem: Your team must fix tray 6 m above the level concrete floor of a warehouse. Which access is usually the best choice?
options: A mobile elevating work platform used by trained operators
A long ladder tied at the top to a tray bracket
A forklift with a pallet for the workers to stand on
A step ladder standing on a pallet to gain height

questions.stem: Why should hand tools be tethered (tied on) when you work from a platform above a walkway?
options: So they are not mixed up with another team's tools
So they do not get lost at the end of the day
So the battery tools stay charged and ready
So a dropped tool cannot fall on someone below

questions.stem: Before drilling a ceiling slab for tray hangers, why do you scan it with a cable and pipe detector?
options: To find the hardest part of the concrete to drill
To avoid hitting hidden cables, conduits or pipes
To measure how thick the ceiling slab is
To check that the drill bit is the right size

questions.stem: A conduit carrying the office lighting circuit runs right where a hanger must be fixed. What must happen before you drill next to it?
options: The circuit is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead
You drill slowly, so the bit stops as soon as it touches metal
You wear rubber gloves and use a cordless drill
The office staff are asked not to use the lights

questions.stem: A 3 m length of 600 mm steel ladder tray is heavy and awkward. How should your team get it up to the work position?
options: One person carries it up the tower ladder, resting on a shoulder
Pass it up the outside of the tower from hand to hand
Plan the lift, using a hoist or platform and enough people
Rest it on the guard rail and slide it into the brackets

questions.stem: Which PPE is needed when cutting galvanised tray with an abrasive cut-off saw?
options: A dust mask only, as the sparks are small
Eye and face protection, ear protection and gloves
Ear protection only, as the tray is thin metal and cuts quickly
Rubber gloves only, in case the tray is live

questions.stem: An aluminium tray is to be fixed outdoors on steel brackets. Why must the maker's isolating washers or matching fixings be used?
options: To make the tray easier to take apart and re-use at a later date
To stop the tray expanding in the hot sun
To stop the bolts working loose from vibration
Two different metals touching can corrode in damp air

questions.stem: Which tray type is the best choice for long spans carrying large, heavy power cables?
options: Wire mesh (basket) tray
Light perforated tray
Solid-bottom tray with a cover
Heavy-duty ladder tray

questions.stem: A solid tray with a cover is chosen for a run in a dusty factory. What effect does the cover have on the power cables inside?
options: They run cooler, so they can carry more current
They lose heat less easily, so may need derating
They need no cable ties, because the cover holds them in place
They can be packed in with no limit on numbers

questions.stem: A cut has been made in hot-dip galvanised tray. After deburring, what should be done to the cut edge?
options: Wrap it in insulating tape to cover the bare metal
Wipe it with oil once and leave it to weather
Treat it with zinc-rich paint as the maker says
Heat it with a torch to spread the zinc over it

questions.stem: Which tray suits a computer room where many small data cables are added and changed often?
options: Wire mesh (basket) tray, which is easy to cut and change
Heavy-duty ladder tray with widely spaced rungs
Steel trunking with lids that are screwed down every 300 mm
Steel conduit with a draw box every metre

questions.stem: A straight tray run is 18 m long. Supports are at 1.5 m centres, with one at each end. How many supports are needed?
The cables on a tray weigh 10.4 kg/m in total. The maker's data gives a safe working load of 25 kg/m at the span you plan. What do you conclude?
options: The tray is within its load, with room for more cables
The tray is overloaded and the span must be halved
The load cannot be judged without the cable colours
The tray must be changed to a wire mesh type

questions.stem: A tray has a usable cross-section of 300 mm × 50 mm. The cables add up to 4 500 mm². What percentage of the space do they fill?
The specification allows a tray to be filled to no more than 40%. Your sum gives a fill of 52%. What is the best action?
options: Fit the cables anyway and use more cable ties
Leave out the earth cables so there is more room for the rest
Use a wider or deeper tray, or a second tray run
Put a cover on the tray so the cables stay in

questions.stem: A straight run made of 3 m tray lengths is 24 m long. How many splice joints are needed between the lengths?
Six cables of 25 mm diameter and eight of 15 mm diameter are laid side by side in one layer with no gaps. What is the smallest tray width before spare space is added?
options: 210 mm
240 mm
300 mm
270 mm

questions.stem: A 40 m tray run will cross a rooftop where the metal gets hot in the sun. What does the maker usually ask you to fit along such a run?
options: Expansion splices at the spacing the maker states
An extra cable tie on every rung of the tray
Welded joints in place of the bolted splice plates
A higher torque on every splice bolt

questions.stem: When is a trapeze hanger (two threaded rods and a strut) a better choice than a wall bracket?
options: When the tray runs along the face of a strong concrete wall
When the tray crosses open space under a ceiling
When the tray must be fixed to the floor slab
When the tray is short and carries no cables

questions.stem: A splice joint falls in the middle of a span instead of near a support. What is the risk?
options: The joint is weaker than the tray and can bend there
The joint will lose its earth path when the weather gets hot
The cables will be harder to pull past the joint
The tray will no longer line up with the brackets

questions.stem: An anchor in a concrete ceiling will carry a tray hanger. What decides the anchor's size and depth?
options: The size of drill bit the team has on site
The load it carries and the maker's anchor data
The colour code printed on the anchor box
How quickly the hole can be drilled

questions.stem: Why are lock nuts or double nuts fitted under the strut of a loaded trapeze hanger?
options: To make the hanger look neat from below
So the rod can safely carry twice the load printed on its label
So the strut cannot creep down the rod with vibration
To insulate the strut from the threaded rods

questions.stem: Cables run on a vertical tray from the ground floor up to a roof plant room. How are they best held?
options: Laid loose, as the tray sides will hold them in
Taped to the rungs with insulating tape
Tied only at the top so that they hang straight
Fixed with cleats or ties at close, regular spacing

questions.stem: On a planned job, why are factory-made bends used instead of bends cut and bent from straight tray on site?
options: Site-made bends are always cheaper and quicker
Factory bends need no supports near them
Factory bends never need to be bonded
They keep the maker's strength and bend radius

questions.stem: Splice bolts must be tightened to the maker's torque. What can happen if they are left loose?
options: The tray becomes too stiff and may crack
The cables are squeezed and their insulation is cut at the joint
The joint can move and the earth path can fail
The zinc coating melts at the joint

questions.stem: A tray must rise 600 mm to pass over a duct and then drop back down. Which fittings are used?
options: A tee and a cross
Vertical riser bends
Horizontal bends
A reducer and an end cap

questions.stem: The specification says the tray is not to be used as a circuit protective conductor, but it must be bonded. What does this mean?
options: Each circuit has its own earth conductor, and the tray is earthed too
The tray carries the fault current for every circuit laid in it
The tray is insulated and must never be connected to earth
Only the first length of tray needs an earth connection

questions.stem: A continuity test along a 30 m bonded tray run gives a reading much higher than the rest of the system. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cables in the tray are too large
A splice joint is loose, painted or dirty
The tray is fixed to a concrete wall
The test leads were nulled before the test

questions.stem: Why are paint and dirt cleaned off where a bonding jumper is fixed to a tray?
options: So the jumper sits flat against the tray and looks neat to the client
So the bolt can be tightened by hand
So the paint does not rub off on the cables
So there is a good, low-resistance metal contact

questions.stem: Where should the tray's bonding continuity results be recorded?
options: On a note kept in the tester's case
On the back of the job drawing only
On the test record in the handover file
On the tray itself, in marker pen

questions.stem: Why are cable rollers set up along a tray before a long, heavy cable is pulled in?
options: To cut friction and stop the sheath being damaged
To hold the tray down while the cable is pulled
To measure the length of cable pulled in
To keep the cable warm so that it bends easily

questions.stem: A power cable and an instrument signal cable must share a tray route. What is the usual good practice?
options: Twist them together so they stay tidy
Lay the signal cable on top of the power cable
Separate them with a barrier or keep them apart
Tie them tightly into the same bundle at every metre

questions.stem: Why are large power cables on a ladder tray laid in a single layer, or spaced, as the cable data says?
options: So heat can escape and the cables keep their rating
So the cables are easier to count at handover
So the tray needs fewer splice plates
So the cables can be painted later

questions.stem: Which ties are the right choice for cables on an outdoor tray in full sun?
options: Any plastic ties, as long as they are tight
UV-resistant plastic or stainless steel ties
Paper-covered garden wire ties
Insulating tape wrapped twice round

questions.stem: A cable has been pulled round a tray bend tighter than its data sheet allows. What should you do?
options: Leave it, as the tray bend will hold it in shape
Tape the bend in place so that the cable cannot move any further
Heat the cable so that it relaxes into the bend
Ease it out to at least the stated minimum radius

questions.stem: At the final inspection you find a hanger where the nut has caught only a few threads of the rod. What should you do?
options: Record it and have it put right before handover
Leave it, because the tray is already loaded
Paint the nut so the fault does not show
Tell the client to check it in a year

questions.stem: Why are 'as-built' drawings marked up at the end of a tray job?
options: To show the client the tray maker's prices
To show where the team took its breaks
To prove that the tray was painted
To show where the tray was actually installed

questions.stem: The tray passes through a fire-rated wall. Why is the fire-stopping photographed and recorded before the ceiling is closed?
options: To show the client the colour of the sealant
So there is proof it was done to the approved method
So more cables can be pushed through it easily later
Because the sealant must be removed after a week

questions.stem: You lead a team of four. One trainee has fixed brackets 20 mm out of line along the run. What is the best way to deal with it?
options: Leave it, as the cables will hide the error
Fix the rest of the run to match the wrong ones
Stop, show how to set out from the line, and correct them
Report the trainee to the client and carry on with the run

questions.stem: Which items belong in a good handover pack for a tray installation?
options: The tray maker's price list and order forms
Test records, as-built drawings and maker's data
The spare splice bolts and leftover cable ties
A copy of the team's attendance sheet

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A straight tray run is 21 m long, with supports at 1.5 m centres and one at each end. How many supports are needed?
The cables on a tray weigh 6 kg per metre in total. The supports are 2 m apart. What weight of cable, in kilograms, does one span carry?
A tray is 300 mm wide and 50 mm deep inside. The cables in it add up to 6 000 mm². What percentage of the space is filled?
What is the name of the splice plate that lets two tray lengths slide a little, so a long run can grow and shrink with heat?
What is the name of the corrosion that happens when two different metals touch in damp or salty air?
What kind of paint is used to touch up the cut edge of hot-dip galvanised tray?
What do the letters MEWP stand for?
What is the word for the distance between the centres of two tray supports?
In what unit is a tray's safe working load usually given in the maker's tables?
What is the name of the fitting where four tray runs meet at one point?
What is the name of the radiation in sunlight that breaks down plastic cable ties and sheaths over time?
What are the free-turning wheels called that are set along a tray so a cable can be pulled in without dragging?
What is the name of the metal strip fitted along a tray to keep power cables apart from data cables?
A straight run made of 3 m tray lengths is 27 m long. How many tray lengths are needed?
Which instrument is used to test the continuity of the bonding along a metal tray run?

essays.stem: You are to lead the installation of a 60 m cable tray system in a new warehouse in Portmore. Explain how you would plan the job before any tray is fixed.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the drawings and the specification to find the tray type, size, finish, fixing heights, spare capacity and support method, and raise a query on anything unclear or in conflict. I would walk the route with the other trades' drawings to find beams, ducts, pipes and sprinklers in the way, and agree the final route and levels. From the drawings I would do a take-off of tray lengths, bends, tees, risers, splices, supports, anchors and bonding jumpers, and check the cable schedule so the tray width, fill and load are right. I would plan access (a MEWP or towers), lifting, storage of the tray on site and the order of work. I would write a risk assessment and method statement, list the isolations needed for nearby circuits, brief the team, and plan the inspection and test records for handover.
markingPoints: Reads the drawings and specification and raises queries on conflicts
Surveys the route with other trades' drawings and agrees clashes
Makes a full materials take-off and checks width, fill and load against the cable schedule
Plans access, lifting, storage and the order of work
Prepares the risk assessment, method statement, isolations, team briefing and records

essays.stem: Compare ladder tray, perforated tray, wire mesh tray and solid covered tray, and say which you would choose for (a) heavy power cables in a factory, (b) data cables in an office, and (c) a run on a hotel roof near the sea.
essays.modelAnswer: Ladder tray has two side rails and rungs. It is strong over long spans and lets air reach the cables, so it suits large power cables; for a factory (a) I would choose heavy-duty galvanised ladder tray. Perforated tray has a flat, holed base that supports small cables along their length and still lets some air through. Wire mesh tray is light, easy to cut and change, and supports many small cables, so for office data cables (b) I would choose mesh tray, kept apart from power. Solid tray with a cover protects cables from dust, sun and falling objects, but holds heat in, so cables may need derating. For a sea-front roof (c) the material matters most: I would choose stainless steel or fibreglass tray with matching fixings, and perhaps a cover to shade the cables, with UV-resistant ties.
markingPoints: Describes ladder tray and chooses it for heavy factory power cables
Describes perforated and mesh tray and chooses mesh (or perforated) for office data
Describes solid covered tray, its protection and its heat effect (derating)
Chooses corrosion-resistant material (stainless or fibreglass) with matching fixings for the sea-front roof
Mentions UV-resistant ties or shading for the outdoor run

essays.stem: A 15 m tray run will carry cables weighing 14 kg/m in total. The maker's table gives a safe working load of 30 kg/m at 2.0 m spans and 18 kg/m at 3.0 m spans. Explain which span you would choose, how many supports you need, and what else you would check. Show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: At 3.0 m spans the tray can carry 18 kg/m. The cables weigh 14 kg/m, which is within the limit but leaves only 4 kg/m, so there is little room for future cables or a person's accidental weight. At 2.0 m spans the limit is 30 kg/m, which leaves 16 kg/m spare. I would choose 2.0 m spans, which also suits the spare capacity in most specifications. For 15 m at 2.0 m spans, 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5, so I round up to 8 spans and need 9 supports, one at each end, with the spacing set a little under 2 m. I would also check that each support, anchor and threaded rod can carry its share of the load from the maker's data, put supports near bends, tees and splices as the maker says, check the tray fill, and record the calculation for the file.
markingPoints: Compares the cable load with both table values correctly
Chooses the 2.0 m span and gives a sound reason (spare capacity)
Works out the number of supports correctly (9) and rounds up
Checks supports, anchors and rods against the maker's data
Mentions supports near fittings, fill check and recording the calculation

essays.stem: Explain how you would make sure a long metal tray system is bonded to earth along its whole length, and how you would test and record it.
essays.modelAnswer: A metal tray can become live if a cable is damaged, so it must be connected to the earthing system so that a fault will operate the protection. I would follow the specification and the maker's instructions. Each splice is bolted with the maker's plates and bolts at the right torque, on clean metal. Where a joint cannot be relied on, such as an expansion splice, a painted joint or a change of material, I fit a bonding jumper across it with clean contact faces. The tray is connected to the main earthing terminal or the earth bar at the board with a suitable conductor. With all circuits on the tray isolated or not yet connected, I test continuity from the earthing point to the far end and to each branch, using a low-resistance ohmmeter with its leads nulled. A reading much higher than the rest points to a bad joint, which I fix and retest. I write the results on the test record for the handover file.
markingPoints: Explains why the tray must be earthed (fault will operate protection)
Splices bolted to torque on clean metal, as the maker says
Bonding jumpers across expansion splices, painted joints or doubtful joints, and a connection to the main earth
Tests end-to-end continuity with a nulled low-resistance ohmmeter and investigates high readings
Records the results for handover

essays.stem: Your team will fix tray at 5 m in a busy workshop in May Pen. Explain how you would plan and control the work at height.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first ask if any work can be done at ground level, such as assembling trapeze hangers and splicing tray lengths. For the rest I would choose the access: a MEWP if the floor is level and strong and trained operators are available, or mobile towers with guard rails, wheels locked and built by a competent person. I would check the access equipment before each use and make sure the inspection tag is in date. I would set an exclusion zone with barriers and signs under the work, agree times with the workshop supervisor, and keep people out of the zone. Tools would be tethered and materials kept in a tray or bag. I would plan how heavy tray lengths are lifted, with a hoist or enough people. There would be a rescue plan for anyone stuck at height. I would brief the team, supervise closely and stop work if conditions change.
markingPoints: Reduces work at height by assembling at ground level where possible
Chooses suitable access (MEWP or tower) and checks it before use
Sets an exclusion zone below and coordinates with the workshop
Prevents falling objects and plans the lifting of tray
Rescue plan, team briefing and supervision

essays.stem: Explain why power, control and data cables are kept apart on cable trays, and describe how you would arrange them on a shared route.
essays.modelAnswer: Power cables carry large currents that make magnetic fields and electrical noise. Data and control cables carry small signals, so the noise can cause errors, false readings or lost data. A fault in a power cable could also damage the smaller cables or put a dangerous voltage on them. For safety, cables of different voltage bands should not be mixed unless they are insulated for the highest voltage present. On a shared route I would use separate trays where possible, for example with power on the top tray and data on a lower one, or a tray with a fixed metal divider. I would keep the separation distance the specification gives, cross power and data cables at right angles where they must cross, and keep each group neatly laid and tied. I would label the trays or sections so later workers keep the cables apart.
markingPoints: Explains that power cables cause interference on data and control cables
Explains the safety reason (faults, different voltage bands)
Uses separate trays or a fixed divider
Keeps the specified distance and crosses at right angles
Lays the cables neatly and labels the sections

essays.stem: Explain why long tray runs need provision for expansion, and how you would provide it where the tray crosses a building's expansion joint and along a sunny rooftop.
essays.modelAnswer: Metal gets longer when it heats and shorter when it cools. On a rooftop in Jamaica the tray can get very hot by day and cool at night, so a long run moves a lot. If it cannot move, it can buckle, pull its supports loose or break its splices. A building also has expansion joints where two parts of the structure move separately, and a tray fixed rigidly across one can be torn. I would follow the maker's instructions: fit expansion splices at the spacing the maker gives on long outdoor runs, and one where the tray crosses the building joint. Supports near an expansion splice must let the tray slide, using guide clamps instead of tight hold-down clamps. Cables must have some slack at the joint. Because an expansion splice may not give a good earth path, I fit a flexible bonding jumper across it and test continuity.
markingPoints: Explains thermal expansion and its effects (buckling, loose supports, broken splices)
Explains building expansion joints
Fits expansion splices at the maker's spacing and at the building joint
Uses sliding or guide supports and leaves cable slack
Fits a bonding jumper across the expansion splice and tests it

essays.stem: Describe how you would lead a team pulling a heavy armoured power cable onto a 40 m tray run with two bends.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check the cable schedule for size, length and route, and check the cable data for its minimum bending radius and weight. The drum is set on a stand or jacks at the start of the run, so the cable comes off the top in the right direction, with a brake person at the drum. Rollers are set along the straight runs and corner rollers at each bend, so the cable keeps at least its minimum radius. I would place a person at each bend with a clear way to signal, and agree simple calls such as 'pull' and 'stop'. The cable is pulled steadily by hand or a winch with a tension limit, never jerked. As it lies in place it is lifted off the rollers onto the tray, laid straight, spaced as the data says, and tied or cleated. The ends are sealed until termination. I would check the sheath for damage and record the cable as installed.
markingPoints: Checks the schedule and cable data (radius, weight, length)
Sets up the drum, brake and rollers, including corner rollers at bends
Places people at bends with agreed signals
Pulls steadily with controlled tension and keeps the bend radius
Lays, spaces and fixes the cable, seals the ends, checks for damage and records it

essays.stem: Your team has finished a 60 m tray system in a warehouse. Explain how you would organise the final inspection and snagging, and what records you would hand to the client.
essays.modelAnswer: I would walk the whole route with the drawings and specification. I would check that the tray is the right type, size and finish, at the right height and line, straight and level, with no sharp edges and with cut edges treated. Every support would be checked for position, span, fixing and tight nuts, with supports near bends, tees and splices. Splice bolts would be checked for torque, and bonding jumpers for being in place. I would check cable fill, segregation, bend radii and fixing, and that fire-stopping is done where the tray passes through fire-rated walls. I would review the continuity test results. Any faults go on a snag list, are put right and are rechecked. The handover pack would hold the as-built drawings, the test records, the inspection checklist, photos of hidden work such as fire-stopping, and the maker's data and load tables.
markingPoints: Checks type, size, line, level and finish against the drawings
Checks supports, spans, fixings and splice torque
Checks fill, segregation, bend radius, fixing and fire-stopping
Uses a snag list, corrects faults and rechecks
Hands over as-built drawings, test records, inspection checklist, photos and maker's data

essays.stem: The tray route in an occupied office runs through a ceiling space that already holds live lighting and power circuits. Explain how you would work safely there.
essays.modelAnswer: I would never work on or near live conductors. First I would survey the ceiling space and use the drawings and a cable detector to find the existing circuits and where the tray supports will go. I would plan with the client which circuits must be switched off and when, so the office can carry on with as little disruption as possible. Each circuit near the work is isolated at the board, locked off and tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Where a circuit cannot be switched off, I would change the route or support positions to keep well clear of it, or stop and refer it to the supervisor. I would check that ceiling tiles and grids are not overloaded, keep the area below fenced off, and record the isolations. When the work is done the supply is restored only by the authorised person, after checking that all tools and off-cuts are out.
markingPoints: Surveys and locates existing circuits with drawings and a cable detector
Plans outages with the client
Isolates, locks off, tags and proves dead with a tester checked before and after
Reroutes or stops if a circuit cannot be isolated; never works live
Protects the area below, records the isolations and restores the supply properly

practical1.title: Plan, set out and install a tray system with a riser and an expansion splice, and test its bonding
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing and specification for a tray system on the Centre's training wall and ceiling frame: a straight ladder tray run of about 6 m along the wall, a horizontal bend, a pair of vertical riser bends to clear an obstruction, and an expansion splice. No circuit on the frame is connected to a supply. As a group: (1) read the drawing and specification, and write a materials take-off and a support calculation (number of supports, span, load against the maker's table the assessor gives); (2) write a short method statement and risk assessment, including access and lifting; (3) set out the line and support positions with a laser level or chalk line; (4) fix the brackets and hangers, cut tray to length, deburr and treat the cut edges, and assemble the run with the maker's splices torqued to the stated value; (5) fit bonding jumpers across the expansion splice and any doubtful joint, and connect the tray to the frame's earth terminal; (6) test continuity end to end with a low-resistance ohmmeter and record it; and (7) inspect the work against the drawing and make a snag list. The team leader for each step is a different member, and every member cuts, fixes or tests at least one part while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage and hand in the take-off, calculation, method statement, test record and snag list.
materials: Training wall and ceiling frame (not connected to any supply)
Drawing, specification and the maker's load and span table from the assessor
Ladder tray lengths, horizontal bend, two vertical riser bends, splice plates, an expansion splice and bolts
Wall brackets, strut channel, threaded rod, nuts and washers, and anchors
Hacksaw or cut-off saw, file, zinc-rich paint and brush
Laser level or chalk line, tape measure, spirit level
Drill with suitable bits, spanners and a torque wrench
Bonding jumpers and an earth conductor with lugs
Low-resistance ohmmeter
Mobile tower or podium steps, as the Centre provides
Method statement, test record and snag list forms
photos: The set-out line and marked support positions
Brackets and hangers fixed, before the tray goes on
A cut edge deburred and treated
The riser bends and expansion splice fitted, with the bonding jumper
The continuity test being carried out, and the completed test record
The finished tray run checked with a level
The snag list and the area cleaned up
checklist: Worked out the number of supports and checked the load against the maker's table correctly
Set out a straight, level line and support positions as the drawing shows
Fixed supports firmly at the right spacing, with supports near bends and splices
Cut, deburred and treated tray edges safely, wearing the right PPE
Assembled splices and the expansion splice as the maker says, torqued to the stated value
Fitted bonding jumpers on clean metal and tested continuity correctly with nulled leads
Led their step clearly and checked the work of others
Worked safely at height and kept the area below clear
safety: The frame is never connected to a supply; scan for hidden services before drilling
Use the tower or podium steps as trained, with wheels locked and guard rails fitted
Wear safety glasses, gloves and ear protection when cutting and drilling
Lift tray lengths with two people and keep the area below barriered off
Collect off-cuts and filings straight away; they are sharp

practical2.title: Lead a cable installation onto a segregated tray, with fill and load checks and a handover pack
practical2.brief: The Centre's training frame has a perforated tray on trapeze hangers, about 4 m long, with a fixed divider, a tee and a drop-out to a training board. No cable is connected to any supply at any time. The assessor gives the group a cable schedule with three power cables, two control cables and two data cables, with their diameters and weights. As a group: (1) work out the tray fill and the cable load per metre, and decide whether the tray is suitable, showing the working; (2) plan the cable pull: drum position, rollers, who stands where and the signals; (3) pull in and lay the cables, power on one side of the divider and control and data on the other, keeping each cable's minimum bending radius; (4) fix the cables with suitable ties at even spacing and protect them where they drop out to the board; (5) label each cable at both ends from the schedule; (6) seal a practice penetration through the frame's fire-stop panel, as the assessor shows; and (7) inspect the work, mark up an as-built drawing and put together a handover pack. Each member leads one stage and takes part in the pull. Photograph each stage and hand in the calculations, pull plan, as-built drawing and handover pack.
materials: Training frame with perforated tray, trapeze hangers, a divider, a tee and a drop-out (not connected to any supply)
Cable schedule with diameters and weights, from the assessor
Short lengths of power, control and data cable on reels
Cable rollers or smooth guides
Cable ties (UV-resistant), cable labels and a marker
Drop-out fitting or edge protection
Practice fire-stop panel and the Centre's practice sealant or pillows
Tape measure, side cutters, scissors
As-built drawing sheet, inspection checklist and handover pack folder
photos: The cable pull plan and the rollers set out
Cables being pulled in, with each member in position
Power and control/data cables laid on either side of the divider
Cables tied, labelled and protected at the drop-out
The marked-up as-built drawing and the handover pack
checklist: Worked out the fill percentage and load per metre correctly and drew the right conclusion
Planned the pull with clear roles and signals
Pulled cable steadily without kinks, keeping the minimum bend radius
Kept power cables apart from control and data cables
Tied cables neatly at even spacing and protected them at the drop-out
Labelled cables correctly from the schedule
Carried out the inspection and marked up the as-built drawing accurately
Led their stage clearly and worked safely with the team
safety: No cable is connected to any supply during the task
Keep hands clear of the rollers and the drum while cable is moving
Lift reels with two people or use a reel stand
Wear gloves when handling cable and cutting ties; cut tie tails flush so no sharp ends are left
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for the fire-stop sealant
